title: Apartheid
description: South African system of racial segregation
wiki_lead:
Apartheid ( ə-PART-(h)yte, especially South African English:  ə-PART-(h)ayt, Afrikaans: [aˈpart(ɦ)əit] ; transl. "separateness", lit. 'aparthood') was a system of institutionalised racial segregation that existed in South Africa from 1948 to 1994. It also existed in South West Africa (now Namibia). It was characterized by an authoritarian political culture based on baasskap (lit. "boss-ship" or "boss-hood"), which ensured that South Africa was dominated politically, socially, and economically by the nation's minority white population. Under this minoritarian system, white citizens held the highest status, while other groups were classified as Indian/Asian, Coloured and Black African, with differing rights and privileges. 
Broadly speaking, apartheid was delineated into "petty apartheid", which entailed the segregation of public facilities and social events, and "grand apartheid", which strictly segregated housing and employment opportunities by race. Public facilities were often just divided into those for Whites and those for "Non-Whites". The first apartheid law was the Prohibition of Mixed Marriages Act, 1949, followed closely by the Immorality Amendment Act of 1950, which made it illegal for most South African citizens to marry or pursue sexual relationships across racial lines. The Population Registration Act, 1950 classified all South Africans into racial groups based on appearance, known ancestry, socioeconomic status, and cultural lifestyle: "Black", "White", "Coloured", and "Indian". 
Places of residence were determined by racial classification. Between 1960 and 1983, 3.5 million Black Africans were removed from their homes and forced into segregated neighbourhoods as a result of apartheid legislation, in some of the largest mass evictions in modern history. Most of these targeted removals were intended to restrict the black population to ten designated "tribal homelands", also known as bantustans.
Apartheid sparked significant international and domestic opposition, resulting in some of the most influential global social movements of the 20th century. It was the target of frequent condemnation in the United Nations and brought about extensive international sanctions, including arms embargoes and economic sanctions on South Africa. Internal resistance to apartheid became increasingly militant during the 1970s and 1980s, prompting brutal crackdowns by the National Party-led government and protracted sectarian violence that left thousands dead or in detention. Some reforms of the apartheid system were undertaken, including allowing for Indian and Coloured political representation in parliament, but these measures failed to appease most activist groups.
Between 1987 and 1993, the National Party entered into bilateral negotiations with the African National Congress (ANC), the leading anti-apartheid political movement, for ending segregation and introducing majority rule, leading to non-racial elections in April 1994. 
Since the end of apartheid, elections have been open and competitive, and the lives of South Africans have improved across multiple metrics. The economic legacy and social effects of apartheid continue to persist to the present day, particularly inequality.

Precursors

Apartheid is an Afrikaans word meaning "separateness", or "the state of being apart", literally "apart-ness" or apart-hood" (from the Afrikaans suffix -heid). Its first recorded use was in 1929. 
Racial discrimination against Black people in South Africa dates to the beginning of large-scale European colonisation of South Africa with the Dutch East India Company's establishment of a trading post in the Cape of Good Hope in 1652, which eventually expanded into the Dutch Cape Colony. The company began the Khoikhoi–Dutch Wars in which it displaced the local Khoikhoi people, replaced them with farms worked by White settlers, and imported Black slaves from across the Dutch Empire. grok_lead: Apartheid was a system of institutionalized racial segregation and discrimination enforced in South Africa from 1948 to the early 1990s by the National Party government, with application also extended to South West Africa (now Namibia) under South African administration. The term apartheid, meaning "apartness" in Afrikaans, formalized and intensified earlier segregation practices through a comprehensive framework of laws that classified people into racial groups (primarily white, black, coloured, and Indian), restricted their movements, residences, and rights, and aimed to preserve white minority rule over political, economic, and social life. Rooted in the ideology of separate development, promoted especially under Prime Minister Hendrik Verwoerd from 1958, the system ostensibly granted each racial group autonomy in designated areas while in practice allocating disproportionate land, resources, and opportunities to the white minority and relegating non-whites to inferior status and limited political participation. Implemented after the National Party's 1948 election victory, apartheid built on pre-existing segregationist measures, such as the 1913 Natives Land Act and urban influx controls, but expanded them into a rigid state-enforced structure. Key legislation included the Population Registration Act (1950), which classified every individual by race; the Group Areas Act (1950), which enforced residential segregation and led to forced removals of millions from urban areas; the Prohibition of Mixed Marriages Act (1949) and Immorality Amendment Act (1950), banning interracial relationships; and the Promotion of Bantu Self-Government Act (1959), which established ethnic "homelands" or Bantustans for black South Africans, denying them citizenship rights in "white" South Africa and confining their political expression to these underdeveloped territories. These laws created a society where non-whites faced restricted access to education, skilled employment, public facilities, and voting rights, while the state used armed repression to maintain control. The system generated widespread internal resistance from organizations such as the African National Congress (ANC), founded in 1912, the Pan Africanist Congress (PAC), the Black Consciousness Movement, and others, through campaigns including the 1952 Defiance Campaign, strikes, protests, and armed struggle after the banning of major groups in 1960. Iconic figures like Nelson Mandela, imprisoned for much of the period, symbolized the opposition. Internationally, apartheid drew condemnation, especially after events like the 1960 Sharpeville massacre, leading to United Nations calls for sanctions, cultural boycotts, and economic pressure, including the U.S. Comprehensive Anti-Apartheid Act of 1986. Internal unrest, economic strain, and the end of the Cold War eroded support for the regime. Under President F.W. de Klerk, reforms began in 1989â1990, including unbanning the ANC, releasing Mandela on February 11, 1990, and negotiating an end to apartheid. This culminated in South Africa's first non-racial democratic elections in April 1994, with Mandela elected as president, marking the formal transition to democracy. Apartheid's legacy persists in ongoing economic inequalities, social divisions, and efforts toward reconciliation, such as the Truth and Reconciliation Commission.
